screens.title: Why auditing and logging matter
screens.narratorSegment: Auditing and logging are the structured processes we use to record who did what, when, and where in a data platform. Auditing is the review and verification of those records to establish accountability. Logging is the systematic capture of events—queries executed, logins attempted, grants changed, and reads or writes performed. Together they answer critical operational questions like who accessed a sensitive table, which query consumed the most resources, and when a change occurred. A concrete example: if a sensitive column is exposed, logs from ACCESS_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY let you trace which account, role, or query read that column and at what time. A common misconception is to treat logging as optional or purely for diagnostics. In practice, logs are legal and operational evidence. For compliance frameworks such as GDPR or HIPAA, logs help demonstrate that access controls work and that you can produce an access history when required. Key practical points: logs must be stored long enough to meet policy, you should prefer account-wide views for cross-database incidents, and you should plan retention and review cadence. Ask yourself: can you demonstrate who accessed a table in the window your policy requires?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Why auditing and logging matter
Definition

Auditing and Logging

Logging captures events like queries and logins. Auditing is the structured review of those logs to prove who did what and why it matters.

Concrete example
If a row is unexpectedly changed, QUERY_HISTORY identifies the query and user that performed the update, giving you an audit trail to investigate.
Common misconception
Logs are not optional diagnostics; they are often required evidence for compliance and incident response.
Key takeaway
Design collection and retention so you can answer security and compliance questions within policy timelines.
Annotated flow
Event generation
Users run queries, authenticate, or change grants, producing log entries.
Collection & storage
Snowflake stores events in INFORMATION_SCHEMA or ACCOUNT_USAGE depending on scope and retention needs.
Audit & response
Analysts query history views to investigate anomalies and produce compliance reports.
Key Takeaway

Treat logs as first-class evidence: retain, review, and connect them to incident response and compliance workflows.

screens.title: ACCOUNT_USAGE vs INFORMATION_SCHEMA
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent confusion is choosing between INFORMATION_SCHEMA and SNOWFLAKE. ACCOUNT_USAGE. INFORMATION_SCHEMA is scoped to the current database and is intended for real-time metadata and recent history. It typically retains a short window of recent events. ACCOUNT_USAGE, on the other hand, is a set of views in the SNOWFLAKE database that provide historical, account-wide telemetry across databases and objects and is the preferred source when you need a longer retention or cross-database visibility. For example, if you need to find all queries by a user across the entire account over the past six months, INFORMATION_SCHEMA will not suffice. Use ACCOUNT_USAGE. A common mistake is trying to rely on INFORMATION_SCHEMA for audits that span databases or require long retention. Another practical point: some ACCOUNT_USAGE views have different retention windows per view, so verify the view you need supports the historical window required for your compliance policy. The right choice supports accurate incident timelines and avoids incomplete evidence in an audit. ACCOUNT_USAGE vs INFORMATION_SCHEMA means information_schema is database-scoped with limited history; account_usage is account-scoped and stores longer-term audit data.. In practical terms, when to use account-wide historical views vs database-scoped metadata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: INFORMATION_SCHEMA is database-scoped with limited history; ACCOUNT_USAGE is account-scoped and stores longer-term audit data.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › ACCOUNT_USAGE vs INFORMATION_SCHEMA
Information Schema
Scope
Database-scoped metadata and recent history, useful for immediate, local queries.
Limitations
Limited retention window and no account-wide coverage; not suitable for long-term audits.
Account Usage
Scope
Views under SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE provide historical, account-wide telemetry for auditing.
Strengths
Longer retention, cross-database visibility, and views like QUERY_HISTORY, LOGIN_HISTORY, and ACCESS_HISTORY (Enterprise+).
Practical rule
For audits that require historical or account-wide evidence, prefer ACCOUNT_USAGE. For quick, local metadata checks, INFORMATION_SCHEMA is fine. Don't assume INFORMATION_SCHEMA will hold months of history.
Example question
Find queries by user across account for 30 days
Use SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY, not INFORMATION_SCHEMA.
Common mistake
Relying on INFORMATION_SCHEMA for long-term audits
This can lead to incomplete audit evidence during investigations.

screens.title: Key ACCOUNT_USAGE views
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake's ACCOUNT_USAGE schema includes several views you will use frequently for auditing and monitoring. QUERY_HISTORY records every query's metadata, including user, role, warehouse, start and end times, duration, and status — it is the primary source for query investigations. LOGIN_HISTORY captures authentication attempts, client IPs, client type, and whether sign-ins succeeded or failed, which is essential when tracking suspicious logins. ACCESS_HISTORY, available in Enterprise Edition and higher, shows reads and writes at table and column level so you can trace data access precisely. GRANTS_TO_ROLES and GRANTS_TO_USERS show privilege assignments and help verify whether roles are configured as your policy expects. TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS and WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY help with storage and cost analysis. A concrete example: to investigate a sudden rise in credits, combine QUERY_HISTORY with WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to correlate expensive queries with warehouse usage. A common misconception is that one view solves all needs — in reality, audits often join several ACCOUNT_USAGE views to build a complete timeline. Key ACCOUNT_USAGE views means query_history and login_history are go-to views for activity; access_history provides row-level reads and writes for enterprise customers.. In practical terms, what each view records and when to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Key ACCOUNT_USAGE views
Primary views and use cases
QUERY_HISTORY
Details about each executed query: user, role, start/end time, duration, and status. Use it for troubleshooting and cost analysis.
LOGIN_HISTORY
Records login attempts with timestamps, client IPs, client type, and success/failure flags for authentication auditing.
ACCESS_HISTORY
(Enterprise+) Tracks read and write operations on tables and columns to show who accessed which data.
GRANTS_TO_ROLES / GRANTS_TO_USERS
Inventory of privileges to verify RBAC configuration during audits.
TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS & WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
Storage and credit usage details for cost and capacity investigations.
Usage tip
Correlation
Join QUERY_HISTORY with WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to map heavy queries to warehouse credit consumption.
Edition note
ACCESS_HISTORY is available in Enterprise Edition and above; plan accordingly if you need row-level access logs.

screens.title: QUERY_HISTORY: inspect past queries
screens.narratorSegment: QUERY_HISTORY is your primary tool for investigating executed S Q L. It includes metadata such as query_id, query_text, user_name, role_name, start_time, end_time, and execution_status. When investigating, filter by user, role, time window, or warehouse to narrow the results. For example, to find all queries run by JOHN_DOE in the last 24 hours, use an ACCOUNT_USAGE query that filters on user_name and uses DATEADD to set the window. The visual code example on the screen shows a complete S Q L snippet you can copy and adapt for your account. A common mistake is relying on the raw query_text alone; also inspect start_time, end_time, and execution_status to determine if a query failed or consumed extensive resources. When you combine QUERY_HISTORY with WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY, you can attribute cost to specific queries. Practice: run a targeted query with ORDER BY start_time DESC and LIMIT to produce a compact incident timeline. Closing thought: can you use QUERY_HISTORY to assemble a timeline that connects a suspicious login to subsequent queries? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › QUERY_HISTORY: inspect past queries
Example query
SELECT
  query_id,
  query_text,
  user_name,
  role_name,
  start_time,
  end_time,
  execution_status
FROM
  SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE
  user_name = 'JOHN_DOE'
  AND start_time >= DATEADD(hour, -24, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY
  start_time DESC;
Investigation tips
  • Filter by user or role to focus scope.
  • Use ORDER BY start_time DESC to build a timeline.
  • Check execution_status for failures or cancellations.
Interpretation
Concrete example
If a query by JOHN_DOE shows long duration and high credits, correlate the query_id with WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to find the cost impact.
Common mistake
Using INFORMATION_SCHEMA here can miss older, account-wide entries. Use ACCOUNT_USAGE for full history.
Key Takeaway

QUERY_HISTORY is the forensic starting point; always include timestamps and status to build a clear incident timeline.

screens.title: LOGIN_HISTORY: investigate sign-ins
screens.narratorSegment: LOGIN_HISTORY records authentication attempts, client IP addresses, reported client types, timestamps, and whether each attempt succeeded. This view is essential when you suspect unauthorized access or when you need to verify remote access patterns. For a practical example, retrieve the most recent successful login events and inspect client_ip and reported_client_type to verify whether a user logged in from expected locations or tools. A common misconception is to only look for failed logins—both successful and failed attempts matter. Successful logins from unusual IPs or unexpected client types can indicate credential compromise even when authentication succeeded. When investigating, sort by event_timestamp descending and use LIMIT to focus on recent activity. If you see repeated failures followed by a success, that pattern suggests brute-force attempts or credential guessing. Ask: can you produce a short list of unusual login events for your security team? In practical terms, use login telemetry to detect suspicious authentication patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › LOGIN_HISTORY: investigate sign-ins
Query example
SELECT
  event_timestamp,
  user_name,
  client_ip,
  reported_client_type,
  is_success
FROM
  SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY
WHERE
  is_success = TRUE
ORDER BY
  event_timestamp DESC
LIMIT 10;
Practical checks
  • Compare client_ip against known corporate ranges.
  • Look for repetition of failed attempts before a success.
  • Flag logins from unusual client types or geographies.
Concrete scenario
A sudden success from an unfamiliar IP followed by high-privilege queries may indicate compromised credentials; use QUERY_HISTORY to follow the trail.
Misconception check
Don't ignore successful logins; they can reveal compromise when paired with subsequent query activity.
Key Takeaway

Use LOGIN_HISTORY to create an access timeline and correlate logins with later data activity for a complete investigation.

screens.title: ACCESS_HISTORY: track data reads and writes
screens.narratorSegment: ACCESS_HISTORY provides detailed information about read and write operations at the table and column levels, and it is available in Enterprise Edition and higher. This view is especially valuable when you need to prove who read a sensitive column, not just who ran a query. screens.title: Time Travel: query and restore past states
screens.narratorSegment: Time Travel is a user-facing Snowflake feature that lets you query, clone, or restore objects as they existed at a prior point in time within a configured retention window. The retention defaults to one day for standard accounts and can go up to 90 days depending on edition and configuration. You can query a table as it appeared five minutes ago using AT with an OFFSET, e. g., AT (OFFSET => -60*5). You can also UNDROP a recently dropped table to restore it, or create a clone from a specific timestamp using CREATE TABLE... CLONE... AT (TIMESTAMP => '2023-10-26 10:00:00'). A practical example is to create a recovery workflow: after detecting an accidental DROP, run UNDROP to restore the table immediately. A typical misconception is to assume Time Travel lasts indefinitely; it does not — configure retention to meet policy. When planning operations, document your retention settings and include Time Travel in your incident runbooks so you can recover confidently within the allowed window. Commands you will use
-- Query data as it appeared 5 minutes ago
SELECT * FROM my_table AT (OFFSET => -60*5);

-- Restore a dropped table

CREATE TABLE my_table_restored CLONE my_table AT (TIMESTAMP => '2023-10-26 10:00:00'::TIMESTAMP);

Quick recovery, point-in-time analysis, and safe cloning for testing prior states.
Retention
Default retention is limited; increase it if your policies require longer recoverability.

Time Travel is not infinite; do not assume data will always be available without proper retention settings.

screens.title: Fail-safe vs Time Travel
screens.narratorSegment: Time Travel and Fail-safe both relate to recovering historical data, but they serve different needs. Time Travel is user-configurable and accessible; you can query, clone, or restore data within the retention window you set. Fail-safe, by contrast, is a non-configurable, seven-day period managed by Snowflake that becomes relevant only after Time Travel retention expires and is intended for catastrophic system recovery. Importantly, Fail-safe is not accessible to users for routine restores or investigative queries — you cannot query Fail-safe contents. A common operational mistake is to treat Fail-safe as a backup you can use casually. It is not. Instead, view Fail-safe as an additional safety net for extreme events; plan your retention settings and backups with Time Travel for normal recovery workflows. For compliance planning, document your retention settings and ensure they align with legal obligations rather than depending on Fail-safe. Fail-safe vs Time Travel means time travel is your immediate, user-accessible recovery tool; fail-safe is snowflake-controlled and reserved for catastrophic recovery after time travel ends.. In practical terms, understand the differences: user-accessible recovery vs snowflake-managed disaster recovery. screens.title: Compliance checklist and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: To meet compliance obligations, combine technical controls with documented processes. Start by enabling the collection and retention that your policy requires — verify Time Travel retention windows and which ACCOUNT_USAGE views retain the necessary history. Regularly export or archive critical audit views if your retention needs exceed built-in windows. Maintain a documented RBAC strategy and periodically review GRANTS_TO_ROLES and GRANTS_TO_USERS to ensure principle of least privilege. Use dynamic data masking or row access policies where appropriate to protect sensitive data in place, and rely on audit logs to show that masking and policies were effective. Operationally, schedule periodic reviews of LOGIN_HISTORY for unusual access, and correlate LOGIN_HISTORY with QUERY_HISTORY and ACCESS_HISTORY to build incident timelines. Finally, codify runbook steps for common recovery actions such as UNDROP and CLONE, so your team can execute restores within retention periods. Log in and run sample queries using different users or roles to populate LOGIN_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY.

USE ROLE SYSADMIN;
SELECT CURRENT_USER(), CURRENT_ROLE(), CURRENT_WAREHOUSE();
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.TABLES;
USE ROLE PUBLIC;
SELECT 1+1;
Step 2 — Inspect logs
Query LOGIN_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY to find recent events, focusing on timestamps and user names.
-- Last 10 successful logins
SELECT event_timestamp, user_name, client_ip, reported_client_type, is_success
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY
WHERE is_success = TRUE
ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC
LIMIT 10;
Step 3 — Simulate incident and recover
Create a table, insert rows, DROP it, then use UNDROP to restore. Alternatively, clone it at a timestamp.
CREATE TABLE important_data (id INT, value VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO important_data VALUES (1, 'Alpha'), (2, 'Beta');
SELECT * FROM important_data;

-- Simulate accidental deletion
DROP TABLE important_data;

-- Recover
UNDROP TABLE important_data;
SELECT * FROM important_data;

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore why auditing and logging are foundational for secure, compliant data operations in Snowflake. You will learn how account-wide audit views capture queries, logins, grants, and access patterns so you can investigate incidents, measure costs, and prove compliance. We'll also work through Time Travel commands that let you recover or inspect historical data, and contrast that user-facing capability with Fail-safe, Snowflake's internal disaster recovery window. A concrete example you will practice is querying QUERY_HISTORY to find recent queries and using LOGIN_HISTORY to inspect login attempts by IP address. We'll also show a small recovery workflow: create a table, drop it by mistake, and then use UNDROP or CLONE with AT to restore a previous state. Along the way, we'll call out common misconceptions, like relying on INFORMATION_SCHEMA for long-term, account-wide history when ACCOUNT_USAGE is the correct source. By the end you will be able to gather audit evidence, recover recent data, and explain why Time Travel and Fail-safe are different tools for different problems.

Over the next screens you will learn four practical skills that matter for security and compliance. First, you will learn to explain why auditing and logging are essential — being able to say who accessed sensitive data and when is a core requirement for incident response and compliance audits. Second, you'll use the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema to retrieve historical telemetry such as query history and login records across the whole account, which is crucial when investigating cross-database activity. Third, you'll gain hands-on experience with Time Travel to query or restore prior states, and you will practice UNDROP and CLONE workflows to recover data quickly. Fourth, you will be able to differentiate Time Travel from Fail-safe and explain when each applies. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the workflow and a verified competency milestone so you can demonstrate the skill.

This screen explains how you'll prove each objective through practical tasks. For auditing, you'll run queries that locate who accessed or modified a table using ACCOUNT_USAGE views and produce a short report. For account telemetry, you'll fetch LOGIN_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY to identify failed logins and long-running queries, then interpret client IPs and user roles. For Time Travel, you'll perform a controlled error: create a small table, insert rows, drop or update them, and then use UNDROP or a CLONE AT timestamp to restore the original state. This demonstrates both analysis and recovery. Finally, to show you understand Fail-safe, you'll explain in writing why it is not a substitute for Time Travel and when to contact Snowflake support. Each task maps to a verified competency: a saved S Q L script, a recovered table, a short incident timeline, and a compliance justification note.

Auditing and logging are the structured processes we use to record who did what, when, and where in a data platform. Auditing is the review and verification of those records to establish accountability. Logging is the systematic capture of events—queries executed, logins attempted, grants changed, and reads or writes performed. Together they answer critical operational questions like who accessed a sensitive table, which query consumed the most resources, and when a change occurred. A concrete example: if a sensitive column is exposed, logs from ACCESS_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY let you trace which account, role, or query read that column and at what time. A common misconception is to treat logging as optional or purely for diagnostics. In practice, logs are legal and operational evidence. For compliance frameworks such as GDPR or HIPAA, logs help demonstrate that access controls work and that you can produce an access history when required. Key practical points: logs must be stored long enough to meet policy, you should prefer account-wide views for cross-database incidents, and you should plan retention and review cadence. Ask yourself: can you demonstrate who accessed a table in the window your policy requires?

A frequent confusion is choosing between INFORMATION_SCHEMA and SNOWFLAKE. ACCOUNT_USAGE. INFORMATION_SCHEMA is scoped to the current database and is intended for real-time metadata and recent history. It typically retains a short window of recent events. ACCOUNT_USAGE, on the other hand, is a set of views in the SNOWFLAKE database that provide historical, account-wide telemetry across databases and objects and is the preferred source when you need a longer retention or cross-database visibility. For example, if you need to find all queries by a user across the entire account over the past six months, INFORMATION_SCHEMA will not suffice. Use ACCOUNT_USAGE. A common mistake is trying to rely on INFORMATION_SCHEMA for audits that span databases or require long retention. Another practical point: some ACCOUNT_USAGE views have different retention windows per view, so verify the view you need supports the historical window required for your compliance policy. The right choice supports accurate incident timelines and avoids incomplete evidence in an audit. ACCOUNT_USAGE vs INFORMATION_SCHEMA means information_schema is database-scoped with limited history; account_usage is account-scoped and stores longer-term audit data.. In practical terms, when to use account-wide historical views vs database-scoped metadata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Snowflake's ACCOUNT_USAGE schema includes several views you will use frequently for auditing and monitoring. QUERY_HISTORY records every query's metadata, including user, role, warehouse, start and end times, duration, and status — it is the primary source for query investigations. LOGIN_HISTORY captures authentication attempts, client IPs, client type, and whether sign-ins succeeded or failed, which is essential when tracking suspicious logins. ACCESS_HISTORY, available in Enterprise Edition and higher, shows reads and writes at table and column level so you can trace data access precisely. GRANTS_TO_ROLES and GRANTS_TO_USERS show privilege assignments and help verify whether roles are configured as your policy expects. TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS and WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY help with storage and cost analysis. A concrete example: to investigate a sudden rise in credits, combine QUERY_HISTORY with WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to correlate expensive queries with warehouse usage. Time Travel is a user-facing Snowflake feature that lets you query, clone, or restore objects as they existed at a prior point in time within a configured retention window. The retention defaults to one day for standard accounts and can go up to 90 days depending on edition and configuration. You can query a table as it appeared five minutes ago using AT with an OFFSET, e. g., AT (OFFSET => -60*5). You can also UNDROP a recently dropped table to restore it, or create a clone from a specific timestamp using CREATE TABLE... CLONE... AT (TIMESTAMP => '2023-10-26 10:00:00'). A practical example is to create a recovery workflow: after detecting an accidental DROP, run UNDROP to restore the table immediately. A typical misconception is to assume Time Travel lasts indefinitely; it does not — configure retention to meet policy. Time Travel and Fail-safe both relate to recovering historical data, but they serve different needs. Time Travel is user-configurable and accessible; you can query, clone, or restore data within the retention window you set. Fail-safe, by contrast, is a non-configurable, seven-day period managed by Snowflake that becomes relevant only after Time Travel retention expires and is intended for catastrophic system recovery. Importantly, Fail-safe is not accessible to users for routine restores or investigative queries — you cannot query Fail-safe contents. A common operational mistake is to treat Fail-safe as a backup you can use casually. It is not. Instead, view Fail-safe as an additional safety net for extreme events; plan your retention settings and backups with Time Travel for normal recovery workflows. For compliance planning, document your retention settings and ensure they align with legal obligations rather than depending on Fail-safe.
